specPoints.text: understand the terms population, community, habitat and ecosystem

primer.text: Ecology runs on four key terms. This note defines population, community, habitat and ecosystem, shows how they nest inside each other from one species to a whole landscape of interacting living and non-living parts, and explains why removing one species shakes the entire community.

lessons.title: The Four Words That Frame Ecology
lessons.opening: Four terms frame every ecological study: a population is one species in one place at one time, a community is every population sharing that area, a habitat is where an organism lives, and an ecosystem is all the biotic and abiotic factors interacting there.
keyPoints: A population is a group of organisms of one species living together in one place at one time.
A community contains every population living in one area at the same time.
A habitat is the place an organism lives in, for example the woodland that badgers, deer, oak trees and ants share.
An ecosystem is all the biotic and abiotic factors interacting within an area at one time, and ecosystems vary in scale from a garden pond to Antarctica.

low.restatement: One species together is a population, all species together are a community, the address is the habitat, and the address plus its conditions is the ecosystem.
low.analogy: A tower block: one family, all families, the building itself, and the building with its heating, water and wiring.
low.examPointer: Match each term to its keyword — species and time for population, all populations for community, place for habitat, biotic plus abiotic for ecosystem.

medium.restatement: The terms nest: populations of every species in an area form the community, the community lives in a habitat, and adding the abiotic factors — light, minerals, water — turns the habitat into an ecosystem, whose scale runs from a garden pond to the whole of Antarctica.
medium.analogy: Matryoshka dolls: each layer fits inside the next, from one species up to the whole interacting system.
medium.examPointer: Since species depend on each other, removing one species can affect the whole community — that is the exam-favourite consequence.

check.stem: Which term names one species living in one place at one time?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
A community bundles every population, not one species.
A habitat is the place itself, not the group.
An ecosystem adds abiotic factors to the living mix.

check.stem: Badgers, deer, oak trees and ants share a woodland. What does the woodland represent to them?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Four species together cannot form one population.
Community names the group of populations, not the place.
Genotype is a genetic term, not a place.

check.stem: What must an ecosystem include that a community does not?

options.text: The abiotic factors, such as light intensity, mineral ions and water availability
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: More species than the community holds
options.explanation: The species set is identical; the factors differ.
Biotic factors alone are the community part.
Ecosystems can be tiny; scale is not the criterion.

check.stem: What happens to a community if one species is removed?

options.text: The whole community can be affected, since species depend on each other
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Interdependence means effects spread.

options.text: Only the removed species is lost
options.explanation: Its partners feel the knock-on effects.
Removal shrinks, not doubles, the community.

check.stem: A garden pond and the whole of Antarctica are both examples of what?

options.text: Ecosystems, showing ecosystems vary greatly in size and scale
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Habitats only, since both are places
options.explanation: Both terms apply, but the contrast demonstrates ecosystem scale.
The abiotic factors make them ecosystems.
Each holds many species.

check.stem: State the definition of a population.
check.modelAnswer: A population is a group of organisms of one species that live together in one place at one time.

check.stem: State the definition of an ecosystem.
check.modelAnswer: An ecosystem is all the biotic factors and abiotic factors interacting within an area at one time.

check.stem: Explain why a community is more than a population.
check.modelAnswer: A community is more than a population because it gathers all the populations of every species sharing the area, not just one species at a time.

check.stem: A student studies all the fish, plants and snails in a pond plus the water and light. Name the terms.
check.modelAnswer: Each species group is a population, all groups together form the community, the pond is their habitat, and the pond plus its non-living conditions is the ecosystem.

glossary.definition: A group of organisms of one species living together in one place at one time.
Every population living in one area at the same time.
The place where an organism lives.
All the biotic and abiotic factors interacting within an area at one time.
